paragraphs.text: This [oolong](oolong:definition), a partly oxidised tea, comes from [Nantou](nantou:where-it-is). Nantou lies in the middle of Taiwan and is the island's only county that does not touch the sea. It is also [Taiwan's biggest tea county](nantou:why-people-value-it). Its land climbs from low hills to cold mountain gardens, and the trade divides its tea country into [low, middle and high belts](nantou:altitude-bands), because the height of a garden decides which style it makes. This record names only the county, not the township, so it does not say which belt the leaf grew in.

It was made in 1979 and rolled, as most [Taiwan oolong](taiwan-oolong:definition) is, so it is now forty-seven years old. Taiwan has a tradition of keeping oolong for years, called [lao cha](taiwan-oolong:ageing), or old tea. A kept tea is roasted again at low heat from time to time to drive out the moisture it takes in, and stored cool, dry, dark and sealed. No standard says when an oolong becomes old. Those who give a figure put it between ten and thirty years, and this tea is well past that.

brewing.text: Ball-rolled Taiwan oolong takes hot water, about 90 to 100°C, a fairly generous amount of leaf and short steeps; the balls open slowly and give many infusions. Roasted Dong Ding takes water from about 95°C to a full boil. Aged oolong takes very hot water, in a pot that holds its heat, clay above all. Oriental Beauty is the exception and takes cooler water, about 80 to 95°C.

notice.text: A smooth, mellow, thick cup with little astringency, often plum or prune, sometimes something like medicinal herbs or ginseng, and an amber to red-brown liquor.
